content: A percentile represents the value below which a specific percentage of observations in a dataset fall. For instance, the 20th percentile is the value below which 20% of the observations are located. Percentiles and the related concept of percentile rank are frequently utilized in descriptive statistics and in the interpretation of scores from norm-referenced tests. The 25th percentile is also referred to as the first quartile, while the 50th percentile is synonymous with the median. There is no universally accepted definition of a percentile, but most definitions produce comparable results when the dataset is large. One common definition calculates the p-th percentile of N ordered values by first determining the rank using the formula ( n = frac{N}{100} , p + frac{1}{2} ), rounding to the nearest integer, and then selecting the value corresponding to that rank. Another widely used method involves linear interpolation between the two nearest ranks instead of rounding. Specifically, if we have N values ( v_1, v_2, v_3, ldots, v_N ), arranged in ascending order, the percentile corresponding to the n-th value is defined as ( p_n = frac{100}{N} , (n frac{1}{2}) ). For example, if ( N = 5 ), the percentile corresponding to the third value is ( p_3 = frac{100}{5} , (3 frac{1}{2}) = 50 ). To calculate the value ( v ) corresponding to a given percentile ( p ), the following approach is used: If ( p leq p_1 ), then ( v = v_1 ). If ( p geq p_N ), then ( v = v_N ). Otherwise, find an integer ( k ) such that ( p_k leq p leq p_{k+1} ), and compute ( v = v_k + frac{N}{100} , (p p_k) , (v_{k+1} v_k) ). When ( p = 50 ), this formula yields the median. If ( N ) is even and ( p = 25 ), the formula provides the median of the first half of the dataset. A related concept is the weighted percentile, which accounts for the total weight of observations rather than their count. In this case, positive weights ( w_1, w_2, w_3, ldots, w_N ) are assigned to the N values. The cumulative weight up to the n-th value is denoted as ( S_n = sum_{k=1}^{n} w_k ). The formulas are then generalized as follows: ( p_n = frac{100}{S_N} , (S_n frac{w_n}{2}) ). ( v = v_k + frac{p p_k}{p_{k+1} p_k} , (v_{k+1} v_k) ). In most spreadsheet applications, there is no built-in function for calculating weighted percentiles, but the method described above can be adapted for such purposes. Percentiles, deciles, and quartiles are interrelated as follows: The 25th percentile (P25) corresponds to the first quartile (Q1). The 50th percentile (P50) is equivalent to the fifth decile (D5), the second quartile (Q2), and the median. The 75th percentile (P75) corresponds to the third quartile (Q3). The 100th percentile (P100) is equivalent to the tenth decile (D10) and the fourth quartile (Q4). Other relationships include: P10 = D1, P20 = D2, P30 = D3, P40 = D4, P60 = D6, P70 = D7, P80 = D8, and P90 = D9. It is important to note that one quartile represents 25 percentiles, while one decile equals 10 percentiles. In practical applications, percentiles are used in various fields. For example, Internet Service Providers (ISPs) often use the 95th or 98th percentile to calculate burstable bandwidth usage. This method excludes the top 5% or 2% of bandwidth peaks in a month, ensuring that infrequent spikes are disregarded and customers are billed more equitably. In medicine, percentiles are commonly employed to assess the relative health of infants and children by comparing their weight and height percentiles.
